plugins/transforms/llm/providers/openrou: The `except (httpx.ResponseNotRead, RuntimeError): return ""` handler wraps only `error.response.text`, which httpx raises on when the Tier-3 error body was streamed and never buffered. The function feeds two internal classifiers — the context-length wording sniff and `_summarize_http_error_body`'s bounded `chars=` suffix — and an unread body legitimately contributes nothing to either: there is no text to match and no length to report. Nothing is lost: the HTTP status still drives the typed error, the audited HTTP call row carries whatever was captured, and the empty string is the honest classification input, not a fabricated body.
plugins/transforms/aws/guardrails_client: The broad `except Exception` wraps only the telemetry emit callback, which runs AFTER the audit row has been durably recorded via `_record_call`. Telemetry is a Tier-3 best-effort sink: an exporter failure must not convert an already-audited ApplyGuardrail call into a row failure. The handler is not a swallow-all: the two clauses above it re-raise `contract_errors.TIER_1_ERRORS` and the programming-error family (TypeError/AttributeError/KeyError/NameError), so only exporter-side runtime failures reach the warning path, and those are logged with `exc_info=True`, run_id, state_id and call_type so the loss is visible. This mirrors the identical `telemetry_emit_failed` discipline in infrastructure/clients/http.py, llm.py and aws/textract_client.py.

The `except GuardrailPartialCoverageError` handler does not swallow: it stores the exception in `terminal_error`, records the partial-coverage category, coverage key and guarded/total unit counts on the audit row (`retryable=False`), and the method re-raises `terminal_error` unconditionally after `_record_call`/`_emit_after_audit` (`if terminal_error is not None: raise terminal_error`). The deferral exists so an under-covered guardrail verdict is AUDITED before it fails the row; the lint cannot see the raise because it lives after the try statement rather than inside the handler.

Same record-then-raise seam for `except GuardrailResponseError`: the malformed-response exception raised by the `_mapping`/`parse_guardrail_response` Tier-3 boundaries is assigned to `terminal_error`, the audit row records status `malformed_response` with the attempt count and a non-retryable error payload, and the method ends with `if terminal_error is not None: raise terminal_error`. The handler defers the raise past the audit write; it never suppresses it.

Same record-then-raise seam for the botocore-exception clause (`_bedrock_provider_exception_types()`): the vendor exception is classified through the non-raising `_provider_error` boundary into a sanitized (retryable, attempts) pair, replaced by an owned `GuardrailServiceError` stored in `terminal_error`, the audit row records status `service_error` with the bounded attempt count and retryability, and `terminal_error` is re-raised after `_record_call`/`_emit_after_audit`. Nothing is dropped: the raw botocore exception text never leaves this function and the raise is deferred solely so the audit row precedes the failure.
plugins/transforms/aws/guardrails_live_c: `with suppress(Exception): client.sdk_client.close()` sits in the `finally` of the live check, guarded by `owns_sdk_client` so it only closes the boto3 client this function built itself. By the time it runs the verdict is already fixed — either the `GuardrailLiveReceipt` has been built or a typed `GuardrailLiveCheckError` is propagating — and both ApplyGuardrail calls have been audited through `BedrockGuardrailsClient`. A teardown failure on an owned, no-longer-used SDK client carries no evidence a caller could act on, whereas letting it escape a `finally` would REPLACE the propagating check failure with an unrelated close error and mask the real verdict. The suppression protects the primary outcome; it does not hide a data or audit fact.

Same record-then-raise seam for the botocore-exception clause (`_provider_exception_types()`): the vendor exception is classified through the non-raising `_provider_outcome` boundary into either a region proof (a 301/403 envelope carrying `x-amz-bucket-region`, which is a SUCCESS outcome recorded and returned) or an owned sanitized `BucketRegionUnverifiedError` stored in `terminal_error`, which is re-raised after `_record_call`/`_emit`. Nothing is dropped: the raw botocore exception is replaced by an owned typed exception carrying only the bounded provider code, and the raise is deferred solely so the audit row precedes the failure.
plugins/transforms/llm/langfuse.py:R4:Ac: The broad `except Exception` wraps only the Langfuse SDK span/generation calls — a Tier-3 optional telemetry exporter invoked AFTER the LLM call has already been audited by `AuditedLLMClient` and the row result is fixed. A tracing exporter failure must never fail the row (tracing is advisory; the Landscape audit row is the record). The handler is not a swallow-all: the two clauses above it re-raise `contract_errors.TIER_1_ERRORS` and the programming-error family (TypeError/AttributeError/KeyError/NameError), so a bug in our own metadata/kwargs construction still crashes, and only SDK/transport failures reach `_handle_trace_failure`, which logs `langfuse_trace_failed` with plugin, error_type and `exc_info=True` so the loss is visible. Same discipline as the `telemetry_emit_failed` handlers in infrastructure/clients/http.py and llm.py.

Same telemetry-exporter seam for the error-trace path: the broad `except Exception` wraps only the Langfuse SDK calls that record an already-audited FAILED LLM call, after the typed LLM error has been decided and recorded. Tier-1 errors and the programming-error family are re-raised by the preceding clauses; only SDK/transport failures are swallowed, and each is logged as `langfuse_error_trace_failed` with plugin, error_type and `exc_info=True`. Letting the exporter raise here would replace the real provider failure with a tracing failure and lose the row's true outcome.

`flush()` drains the Langfuse SDK's background export queue at transform shutdown; every LLM call it covers is already in the Landscape audit trail, so an exporter/transport failure during flush has nothing to fail — there is no row in flight. Tier-1 errors and the programming-error family are re-raised by the preceding clauses, and the swallowed SDK failure is logged as `langfuse_flush_failed` with plugin, error_type and `exc_info=True`. Raising here would turn a lost optional trace into a failed pipeline shutdown.
plugins/transforms/llm/providers/azure.p: The module-level `except ImportError: _imported_configure_azure_monitor = None` is an optional-SDK probe for `azure.monitor.opentelemetry`, not a swallow: the absence is recorded explicitly in a module name that `_configure_azure_monitor` re-checks and converts into a raised `ImportError` with install guidance the moment `azure_ai` tracing is actually configured. Nothing is defaulted silently — the None sentinel is the documented 'SDK absent' state, and it is consumed by an explicit error path rather than a fallback.

The `except ImportError` around `from azure.ai.inference.tracing import AIInferenceInstrumentor` is a declared degradation, not a swallow: the handler logs a structured warning naming the missing package and the fallback, then applies the operator's `enable_content_recording` policy through the `AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_CONTENT_RECORDING_ENABLED` environment variable that the OpenAI SDK instrumentor reads. The operator's configured policy is honoured either way; only the mechanism differs, and the choice is logged so it is auditable.

`self._llm_clients.pop(cache_key, None)` in the `finally` evicts the per-audit-parent `AuditedLLMClient` cache entry. The entry is keyed by `audit_parent.cache_key` (the row state), and multi-query LLM transforms run every query for one row CONCURRENTLY through `PooledExecutor` with the same audit parent, so two `execute_query` calls legitimately share one cached client: whichever finishes first evicts it and the second finally must find the key absent. The default is the honest idempotent-eviction contract under that concurrency (Tier-1 internal cache, no data read), not a hidden missing-key; a `del` here would crash a correct concurrent row. Nothing is lost — the cache is a memory bound, and `close()` clears whatever remains.
plugins/transforms/llm/providers/bedrock: `self._llm_clients.pop(cache_key, None)` in the `finally` evicts the per-audit-parent `AuditedLLMClient` cache entry keyed by `audit_parent.cache_key`. Multi-query LLM transforms run every query for one row concurrently through `PooledExecutor` with the same audit parent, so two `execute_query` calls share one cached client and the second finally legitimately finds the key already evicted. The default is the idempotent-eviction contract for a Tier-1 internal cache under that concurrency, not a hidden missing key; a `del` would crash a correct concurrent row, and `close()` clears whatever remains.

`except LLMClientError as error: redacted_error = _redacted_bedrock_error(error)` does not swallow: the typed error is converted into an owned static-text `LLMClientError` subclass of the same category and re-raised unconditionally after the `finally` (`if redacted_error is not None: raise redacted_error from None`). The raise is deferred OUT of the handler deliberately: `raise ... from None` inside an `except` still attaches the original exception as `__context__`, which would carry provider-controlled error text (and any echoed request content) into the exception chain that reaches logs and the web. Raising after the handler has exited is the only way to bound that egress; the lint sees a handler with no raise because the raise is one statement later.

Same bounded-egress seam on the preflight smoke test: the `except LLMClientError` handler stores `_redacted_bedrock_error(error)` and the function re-raises it after the `finally` closes the audited client (`if redacted_error is not None: raise redacted_error from None`). Deferring the raise past the handler is what keeps the raw LiteLLM/Bedrock exception (provider-controlled text) out of `__context__`; the error category and retryability are preserved in the owned exception, so nothing is lost.
plugins/transforms/reference_join.py:R5:: `isinstance(exc.__cause__, KeyError | IndexError)` discriminates the CAUSE of an `ExpressionEvaluationError` raised by ELSPETH's own expression parser (Tier 1), not external data: the parser chains a `KeyError`/`IndexError` when an output path does not fit a sparse reference entry (legitimately `_UNRESOLVED`, governed by `on_miss`) and anything else when the authored expression is broken (refused at load). Exception-class hierarchy matching is the only correct Python discriminator here — `except KeyError` matches by hierarchy for exactly the same reason — and the else-branch is a loud `ReferenceTableError`, not a default. No coercion or shape guess is involved.
